catalog_quote: Three degrees of stress are recognized: heavy stress ["], primary stress ['], and secondary stress [˚]. Heavy stress is significant within the phonological clause and often coincides with emphasis (see 4.32). Primary stress always occurs on the final syllable of words: /tata/ [ta'ta] 'fire'. audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' final primary stress with alternating secondary leftward (rule 01 101 0101...) rests on Kakumasu 1968 §4.1, and the deciding sentence is on the held typescript scan at p. 15 exactly as quoted (scanned-verified from the image-only PDF). Suffixed words keep final primary stress (suffix takes it), clitics do not perturb it (pp. 15-16), so the WORD domain and strictness are consistent with the source. A second, independent, first-hand description (Caldas 2009 UnB dissertation, §2.3 p. 43) was fetched sources now and confirms final stress, noting only 'a few words' with penultimate stress — a lexical-exception remark that does not change a fixed-final classification but could be recorded in the 'exst'/caution field. Lopes 2009 (held) has no stress section but every stress-marked form is final-stressed. No later phonology or instrumental study appears in Glottolog 5.1 or in Caldas's

sources.citation: Caldas, Raimunda Benedita Cristina. 2009. Uma proposta de dicionário para a língua Ka'apór. Tese de Doutorado, Universidade de Brasília. 334 pp. (open PDF, Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú, etnolinguistica.org/tese:caldas-2009)
sources.quote: "Em Ka'apór observa-se a ocorrência de maior intensidade expiratória na última sílaba da palavra, quando se tem duas ou mais sílabas. Há poucas palavras cuja intensidade expiratória recai na penúltima sílaba." (Word stress = greatest expiratory intensity on the final syllable of words of two or more syllables; a few words have penultimate stress.) All phonemic transcriptions in the chapter mark final stress, e.g. /mo'nok/ 'cortar', /ru'waj/ 'rabo', /tÈapua'pu/ 'trovão'.
